item.content:encoded:
Local design-build studio Allprace aimed to create a feeling of "warmth and permanence" in a house called Hargis, which features gabled roof forms and earthy materials such as wood and stone.

Set within a creative district in Culver City, which is part of Los Angeles County, the project was designed for a client who "values understated luxury, exceptional craftsmanship, and a lifestyle centred around art, nature and walkability," said Allprace.

It is located on a rectangular property that formerly held an ageing house and two-car garage, which were demolished.

In their place, the team created a main residence and a detached guesthouse. Rather than creating a sense of "luxury through excess", the team sought to design a calm, restorative house that was connected to its surroundings.

"Throughout the redesign, founder Shanty and her partner James Mulyadi focused on creating a residence where every material contributes to a sense of warmth and permanence," the team said.

The main dwelling is topped with a prominent roof consisting of gabled and flat elements. Facades are clad in wood and light-toned brick.

The ground level holds an open-concept kitchen, dining area and living room, along with a bedroom and garage.

The upper floor contains bedrooms and a den, and is designed to have a "quieter, more intimate atmosphere dedicated to rest".

In the rear yard, there is a guest house and a small swimming pool, a portion of which is sheltered by the structure's upper level.

Influenced by the concept of biophilia, the architecture studio picked earthy materials such as stone, wood and living plants. An emphasis was placed on craftsmanship and expressing the texture of materials.

Read:

B2A Architects uses concrete columns to elevate Dutch home above dyke

The ground level features limestone flooring, while the upper level has herringbone-patterned wood flooring. The kitchen is fitted with a travertine island and white oak cabinetry.

Notable lighting fixtures include a Bocci chandelier from its 14 Series, which is suspended above a spiral staircase.

Rooms feature custom millwork and ample glazing, including a large triangular window in the primary bathroom.

"One of the home's defining architectural moments is a dramatic, 14-foot by 20-foot triangular window, which floods the interiors with natural light while creating a sculptural focal point visible from both inside and out," the team said.

Other projects in Culver City include a faceted, courtyard-style house by FreelandBuck and a bungalow renovation by Edward Ogosta, which features an extension with a window wall and angled roof.

The photography is by Gavin Cater.

item.content:encoded:
A skyscraper-sized jail designed by architecture studio HOK is undergoing site preparation in New York City's Chinatown as one of the four new borough-based structures designed to replace the city's notorious Rikers Island jail complex.

The Manhattan Detention Facility will be located at 125 White Street in Chinatown, on the same site as the former Manhattan Detention Complex (The Tombs), which was demolished in 2024.

The most up-to-date renders released by the New York City Department of Design and Construction (DDC) and HOK show a building that is 335 feet tall (102 metres) and roughly 13 floors, which aligns with the height of the New York County Criminal Court building next door.

It will be the tallest correctional facility in the world if built to this height, leading to its being dubbed a "jailscraper".

The Manhattan Detention Facility building is split into two main volumes by a walkway that cuts through the bottom of the base and provides a pedestrian passageway across the site.

A reddish mesh screen and undulating panels cover a portion of the facade.

Towards the middle of the building, this "double skin system with security mesh" will act as a viewpoint for those in custody and surround spaces such as the "recreation hall".

"To address privacy, a double skin system with security mesh and architectural screen supports visual privacy by creating a separation between the exterior-most facade and the people in custody," reads a DDC design document.

Cells are located in the upper floors, while the ground level will contain a public lobby, a community and retail space and a staff lobby. Below ground, there will be parking for Department of Correction and New York Police Department staff.

A total of 1,040 beds are planned for the facility.

Read:

Bronx jail designed to be "responsive to the neighborhood"

According to the DDC, the city is still working with the surrounding community and the architecture team to finalise the design, which is updated periodically on the project website.

Per community request, a variety of plantings and some seating will be placed around the site and in the public walkway.

A visitor space that "feels comfortable and supports a welcoming environment" and contains easily accessible lockers and restrooms is also planned for the building per the community's request, according to the DDC.

An assortment of public artwork that previously surrounded the Tombs will be preserved and integrated around the site.

This includes aluminium wire sculptures by artist Kit-Yin Snyder, which stood outside the former entrance, and stone bas-reliefs by Richard Hass, which were encapsulated in the old facade.

Site work on the new Manhattan Detention Facility is underway, including utility work and preliminary excavation. It is slated for completion in 2032.

The jail is one of four in New York City put forward to receive a relocated population from the Rikers Island jail complex. Rikers Island, a small island located in the East River, contains 10 of the city's 15 correctional facilities, which hold up to 15,000 detainees.

It is notorious for its violent environment and inhumane conditions.

In 2019, New York City announced the complex's eventual closure, with plans to disperse the incarcerated population into four smaller jails in Manhattan, Brooklyn, The Bronx and Queens via an initiative called the Borough-Based Jail Program.

HOK is leading the design of the Manhattan and Brooklyn jails, with Cetra Ruddy on The Bronx project and Michael Graves and others on the Queens jail.

Work on all four facilities is underway and in various stages, with the Brooklyn jail the furthest along, topping out just short of the Manhattan jail's planned height at 295 feet (89 metres).

Read:

Nordic model to inform redesign of California's San Quentin prison

The Manhattan jail has drawn much controversy, with the public and community organisations in opposition. Most recently, local leaders penned a letter to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, warning of the site's structural fragility and calling for a reevaluation of the location.

"If foundation problems on this site delay or derail construction of the Manhattan facility, the four-borough program cannot absorb the Rikers population and closing Rikers will slip further out of reach," it reads.

Renderings of the Bronx Detention Center by CetraRuddy were made public last year. It is designed to be "responsive to the neighbourhood" and is made up of a stepped volume wrapped in a similar mesh screen as the Manhattan complex.

Some architecture studios have said that design can aid in creating more humane conditions for those incarcerated, while others, such as architect Michael Ford, have called on the design community to stop designing jails and prisons outright.

The images are by HOK, courtesy of the New York City Department of Design and Construction.

Dezeen Showroom: industrial designer Christian Haas has created two new bathroom products for German brand Villeroy & Boch, incorporating delicate ceramic reliefs and open shelving.

Artis Sense is a washbasin with a textured surface informed by pleated textiles, while Artis Frame is a lightweight twist on conventional bathroom furniture, with a metal frame and open structure.

Artis Sense is crafted from premium ceramic material that is highlighted by the fine relief, with light and shadow creating a dynamic ripple across the surface.

An extension of the existing Artis collection, it is available in the same palette of matt colours by designer Gesa Hansen, including bold options such as deep blue Nightfall and vibrant Teal.

Artis Frame, meanwhile, combines the proportions of a washbasin cabinet with a minimal metal frame and optional shelf, creating a visually lightweight option for modern bathrooms.

It can be paired with Artis Sense or one of Villeroy & Boch's other basins and comes in a selection of metal, wood and coloured finishes. These can be optionally coordinated with fittings for a harmonious look.

item.content:encoded:
Indian studio Evolving Radical Aesthetics has completed Ushas, a farmhouse built into a steep Kerala hillside with an open-air temple carved into a retaining wall.

Located in the Malabar hills near Kozhikode, the house was designed for a retired couple who relocated from Andhra Pradesh to cultivate farmland after leaving city life behind.

The home is organised as three staggered volumes, inspired by the region's traditional farmhouses, and positioned to follow the site's contours rather than level them.

"The terrain became our datum. It dictated orientation, levels, movement, structural logic, even materiality," Evolving Radical Aesthetics principal architect and partner Muhammed Ashiqe told Dezeen.

"It's not every day you come across a site so surreal you lose your sense of place," landscape architect and partner AR Rumna said.

"To build is, in itself, an act of harm, so we thought about what was needed and to what extent an untouched piece of land should be disturbed," Rumna continued. "We wanted to build with minimum impact to the site."

The house is built from locally sourced black granite stone laid in thick masonry walls. Above them, a roof made from corrugated galvanised steel sheets, slender steel rafters and traditional Mangalore tiles extends outwards to shelter verandahs from Kerala's heavy monsoon rain.

"We built with locally sourced black granite," Rumna said. "The wall-making imitated the act of cave building – a very basic, primal form of shelter."

"We wanted the house to feel like it's one with the ground, while the light roof ensures that we don't impose anything that would stand out. We wanted the hills to be in the foreground."

A passage running between the stone volumes forms the main route through the house, connecting living spaces, bedrooms and the surrounding farmland.

The passage also leads to a dedicated room for reading and practising the veena – a stringed Indian instrument – which has glazed walls that open directly onto the landscape.

Read:

Summer Home by Mindspark Architects overlooks cardamom plantation in India

Shelters for farm workers sit alongside the main route through the house, reflecting its role as both a home and working farmhouse.

Large openings frame views across the landscape, while verandahs supported by slender metal columns extend the rooms outdoors.

The bedrooms open directly onto sheltered terraces overlooking the hillside, while the living spaces look across the surrounding mountains through full-height glazing beneath the pitched roof.

The building was angled to capture prevailing north-eastern winds, with the granite walls helping to keep the interiors cool.

"Deep overhangs protect the house from rain and sun and also create verandahs to sit out and relax," Ashiqe said.

The steep site's high winds also presented a risk to the Mangalore tiles, so the architects placed a layer of corrugated galvanised steel beneath them to prevent the tiles from breaking or being lifted.

The concealed layer also channels rainwater towards the eaves for drainage.

At the lower level of the site, outside the main house, square-cut granite steps descend to an open-air temple set into the retaining wall.

The living room projects over the shrine above, creating a cantilevered sheltered space for meditation with a stone podium facing the mountains.

"The temple being carved into the retaining wall with the living room cantilevered above is reminiscent of cave temples, a space for solitude and meditation," Rumna said.

"There is also a podium to dance against the backdrop of the mountains, as an offering to the deity."

The surrounding landscape continues the contours of the site with stepped planting beds and walking paths.

Initially built on largely barren ground, the gardens have gradually been planted by the owners with native trees, vegetables and tropical planting, allowing the farmhouse to evolve alongside the land.

Founded by Rumna and Ashiqe in 2012, Evolving Radical Aesthetics is an architecture studio based in Kozhikode, Kerala.

The practice focuses primarily on residential architecture and projects rooted in local climate, materials and topography.

Other homes in Kerala featured on Dezeen include Mindspark Architects' Summer Home, which overlooks a cardamom plantation and opens onto two timber viewing decks through glazed sliding doors.

Another Kerala home that makes use of Mangalore tiles is Ananda by Thought Parallels Architecture, which features a palette of red brickwork, teak wood and carved fretwork panels under an oversized coconut-wood roof.

The photography is courtesy of Evolving Radical Aesthetics.

item.content:encoded:
Pritzker Prize-winning architect Shigeru Ban has completed a wellness hotel on Awaji Island, Japan.

Named the Pasona Natureverse Retreat, the hotel at the tip of Awaji Island near Kobe was designed for long-term stays based on the ideal of Mibyo – an ideal of preventive wellness treatment that translates as "pre-illness".

The hotel is the third project designed by Ban for Japanese company Pasona Group on the island. It follows a thatch-topped restaurant and a wooden meditation retreat.

According to Ban, the hotel's D-shaped form was designed to take advantage of its location between the coast and a forest.

"To express the characteristics of a site defined by these two completely contrasting landscapes, distinct facades were designed for the east and west sides," said Ban.

"Two linear structures with individual qualities are integrated into a single D-shaped plan, flanking a light-filled atrium."

The five-storey hotel was designed primarily for long-term, 30-day-plus retreats, as well as offering shorter stays.

Its 57 rooms are arranged around a large, skylit central atrium with half overlooking the sea and half facing the forest.

While the landward facade is adorned with stylised timber columns, the seaward side was designed to express horizontally, with balconies running the full width on all levels.

"On the seaside, using the seawall as a podium, the facade is highly transparent, featuring four levels of emphasised horizontal slabs that create a seamless continuity between the interior, exterior, and the surrounding scenery," said Ban.

"In contrast to the horizontal emphasis of the seaside, the mountain-side facade features a rhythmic arrangement of timber-clad columns that emphasize a symbolic, somewhat classical vertical structure," he continued.

"At the center, a massive timber canopy and a grand staircase welcome visitors."

Stays at the hotel are focused on preventive wellness treatments, with all guests receiving a personalised wellness program that may include thalassotherapy, hammam meditation, yoga, sound therapy and aromatherapy.

Every room in the hotel contains a private onsen – a natural hot spring bath – and several rooms have sensor-operated beds that monitor nighttime body movement and adjust automatically to encourage the best sleep.

Read:

Shigeru Ban creates wooden Zenbo Seinei retreat on Japanese island

Along with a wellness clinic and treatment room, the hotel includes a dedicated room for aerial yoga with suspended fabric hammocks and a gym.

An indoor swimming pool is fed with salt water from the Seto Inland Sea.

Alongside the wellness facilities, the hotel contains five restaurants, several run by Michelin-starred chefs, as well as several cafes.

On the third floor, an event hall was designed for live musical performances and contains 500 window panes covered in artworks.

One of the world's most respected architects, Ban won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2014 and was recently awarded the 2026 AIA Gold Medal.

He is known for his innovative architecture that often uses cardboard and natural materials, with the Cardboard Cathedral in Christchurch one of his most influential buildings.

The photography is by Hiroyuki Hirai.

item.content:encoded:
Design studios Cella Collective and Mitre & Mondays have designed a timber-framed installation for this year's Houghton Festival in Norfolk, England, covering its walls with thatch sourced from sustainable reedbeds.

Named the Water Tower, the installation provided a restful seating space between the food area and one of the stages at the music and arts event Houghton Festival, which took place from 6 to 9 August.

Cella Collective and Mitre & Mondays' design for the 5.5-metre-tall installation drew upon a water tower built for the nearby Houghton Hall in 1772.

Made from a timber frame, the installation featured four openings separated by slanted walls that were covered in layers of thatch.

A thatched ring topped the structure and wooden seating extended from the walls inside, where visitors could view the circular roof opening above.

"I want people to experience something that looks like it has grown out of the ground – to feel cooled by its shady interior, to feel a connection to it when checking out its handmade flavour," Mitre & Mondays co-founder Josef Shanley-Jackson told Dezeen.

"Thatched structures, inside and out, can feel both contemporary and old-feeling all at the same time," added Cella Collective member Alys Hargreaves.

"It makes sense that we should be revisiting it as a building material which offers a great solution for climate cooling both in the growing of the material and the built structure."

The studios were motivated by regenerative design principles when creating the Water Tower.

The thatch material used in the installation was sourced from reedbeds managed by the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), utilising a by-product material from RSPB's land cutting, which in turn supports the group's conservation efforts and the local wildlife.

Read:

Cob can be "a mainstream building material once again" say Cella

"We centred the whole design around a material ecosystem – reedbed landscapes and the craft of thatching – which aims to support our environment and local building cultures, both of which are under threat or in decline in their own ways," said Hargreaves.

"It has also been an exercise in opposing a culture of convenience where you can only easily buy off-the-shelf items that are part of global supply chains," she continued. "We wanted to learn how we might challenge this and embrace a new material in all its entirety."

Cella Collective and Mitre & Mondays consulted with Cheshire-based master thatchers Wayne Halfpenny and Steve Kelly on the thatching.

"We adopted their intuitive process of crafting with thatch, adapting the design to accommodate the reed," said Cella Collective member Ella Caldicott. "That intuition became part of the build process, with decisions often made through testing and adapting to what was in front of us."

"You can't learn that from reading books; you learn it through your hands and eyes – that's why collaborating with craftsmen and craftswomen is so valuable."

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dezeen (@dezeen)


The thatching was made from reeds sourced from RSPB-managed reedbeds

The Water Tower will be disassembled and reinstalled for future editions of Houghton Festival. Other installations at the festival included a glowing canopy suspended from the trees, which was designed last year by EBBA Architects founder Benni Allan.

We recently rounded up nine contemporary buildings with thatched roofs from around the world, indicating a revival of the age-old craft.

The photography is by Henry Woide.

item.content:encoded:
British studio Richard Parr Associates has renovated a trio of 19th-century buildings at The Newt in Somerset hotel in England, restoring their interiors to nod to the site's past.

Named Yarlington Lodge, the buildings are spread across five hectares of rural land at The Newt in Somerset, a luxury estate, hotel and working farm located just outside of Bruton.

Conceived by Richard Parr Associates as a 32-guest holiday home, the project comprises the main lodge, the Coach House and the Cottage in the Wall – three buildings that historically served as a rectory, its coach house and the gardener's cottage, respectively.

"They were once a functioning trio and we wanted them to become so again," studio founder Richard Parr told Dezeen.

The architect worked with The Newt in Somerset's founders, Koos Bekker and Karen Roos, to restore each property.

For the 1831 lodge, striking patterns and bright colours were selected to reference the high drama of the Napoleonic era.

Bedroom ceilings were clad with swooping textiles that give the impression of military tents, while classical paintings embellish the green-hued library.

Despite these statement design features, Parr explained that interventions to the bones of each building were intentionally subtle. This included carefully restoring the lodge's old fireplaces, elm floorboards and stonework.

"Houses need to retain the spirit of their entire life and should reflect their many owners, hence the references to previous occupants through portraiture and furniture," said the architect.

"The renovation is a mix of little snippets of history with life today," he added.

The Coach House was also adapted to reflect its equestrian history. Blackened steel and raw timber characterise the interior spaces, including the brick-clad living room with a low-slung, beam-lined ceiling.

By contrast, Parr and his team renovated the Cottage in the Wall with sandy-hued walls and wooden accents, which complement the building's lofty ceilings.

Read:

Invisible Studio builds giant window in Somerset hotel garden

"Deliberately pared-back" changes were also made to the facade of each building, Parr said, using local Hadspen stone as well as brick, slate, tile and lead.

"Internally, these same materials were subtly reinterpreted to different levels of sophistication in the form of timber floors, local blue limestone, and a range of pastel colours lifted out of late Regency England," explained Parr.

Alongside the three buildings, the Yarlington Lodge site is home to a rectilinear, tile-clad swimming pool opposite a lush plant-filled greenhouse.

When revitalising the 19th-century properties, Parr described the main hurdle as subtly incorporating air conditioning into the rooms – something he said felt necessary in 2026.

"As the summers get hotter, the need to air-condition all of the bedrooms was introduced into the project," he said. "Devising a way of discreetly housing ducts and grilles into a listed building was extremely challenging."

The Newt in Somerset's sprawling grounds also include a lakeside apiary for honey bees and a rammed earth yoga studio, both designed by Invisible Studio.

The photography is by Ollie Tomlinson.

item.content:encoded:
Architect Alexandre Pavlidis has completed Within the Earth, a house on the Greek island of Sifnos contained within a series of sunken stone walls that step down a coastal hillside.

Referencing the region's use of stepped terraces to grow olives and grapes, Paris-based Alexandre Pavlidis aimed for the home to be "almost invisible", creating subterranean spaces that open out onto expansive, panoramic patios.

"The site is part of a Cycladic landscape structured by agricultural terraces and retaining walls," he told Dezeen. "These walls are not decorative elements; they are what allow the land to be cultivated, to retain soil, and to resist erosion in a rocky and exposed environment."

"In this beautiful nature, the core concept was to create a house that would not appear as a new object in the landscape, but as a continuation of the existing agricultural terraces," he added.

Within the Earth is entered from the base of an existing shepherd's hut at the top of the site, where a staircase leads down into a skylit atrium with a shallow pool of water that separates the bedroom and living spaces.

While the living, dining and kitchen area opens directly onto a large terrace, the bedrooms are set back behind chunky stone supports, which offer privacy to a row of small, private patio spaces.

At the more subterranean back of the home, light is introduced by small, open-air patios planted with trees and, in the bathroom, a cylindrical shower sits beneath a deep skylight.

On the home's lower level, a pavilion-like shelter supported on drystone columns sits alongside a swimming pool set within a second expansive terrace.

Read:

Mold Architects embeds cave-like house in hillside overlooking the Mediterranean Sea

"The visitor leaves the exposed landscape and gradually enters a cooler, darker, more protected world. The house is revealed slowly, through stone, shadow, patios and framed views of the sea," Pavlidis said.

"The communal areas extend lengthwise along the slope, in a way that recalls the linear geometry of the agricultural terraces," he continued. "Patios and skylights bring daylight into the buried plan and create moments where the house opens vertically to the sky."

The rough drystone walls of Within the Earth are complemented by exposed concrete ceilings and polished stone floors.

Contrasting these surfaces are frames, furniture and joinery made of oak, which Pavlidis said helps make the interiors feel "inhabited rather than purely excavated."

On the neighbouring island of Serifos, Greek studio Mold Architects recently completed a hospitality retreat, using stone excavated from the site to form a series of low-lying stepped guesthouses.

The same studio also created a sunken house called NCaved on Serifos, which has a wedge-shaped form embedded into the rocky hillside to shelter it from strong winds.

The photography is by Alexandre Pavlidis unless stated otherwise.

item.content:encoded:
For this roundup, we've collected five smartphones and dumbphones with exciting designs, ranging from a phone with a robot arm to a keyboard phone built for messaging.

For many people, their phone is their most important piece of technology and has been tailored to suit their individual needs. But while the content of our phones is deeply personal, the hardware often feels homogenous and impersonal.

Lately, that's started to change, with technology companies developing phones with more innovative designs and adjustments for people's needs. Here, we've collected some of the most interesting examples from the past year.

Nokia 200 4G, 210 4G, 215 4G 2nd Edition and 235 4G 2nd Edition by HMD

Tech company HMD has released four retro Nokia brick phones, a design that many older mobile phone users remember fondly.

The new design, which has limited internet capabilities, combines the simplicity of the older phones with the functions needed today.

At the centre of the keypad, HMD added a large artificial intelligence (AI) button. This is voice-controlled and can be used to summon a chatbot assistant powered by Shenzhen company Sikey AI.

Find out more about the Nokia AI dumbphone ›

Infinix Note 60 Ultra by Pininfarina

Italian design studio Pininfarina is best known for its car design, but earlier this year it teamed up with Chinese technology brand Infinix to design its first phone.

The Note 60 Ultra has a sleek shape that was intended to evoke the feel of high-speed automotive design. The designers also aimed to get rid of, as much as possible, the "camera bump" to create a more aerodynamic look.

Find out more about the Infinix Note Ultra 60 ›

Clicks Communicator by Clicks Technology

Designed primarily for communication, the Clicks Communicator phone has a QWERTY keyboard on the bottom and was designed for people who enjoy the tactility of physical buttons. It was launched at this year's Consumer Electronics Show.

The phone brings together a user's messages and emails on the home screen. It is also capable of making calls and running other apps, but was mainly created to let users see and respond to messages quickly, without being distracted by other functions.

Find out more about Clicks Communicator ›

Light Flip by Light

The Light Flip brings back a popular old-school phone design – the clamshell-style flip phone. In Light's version, it comes in six colours and runs Light's intentionally stripped-back LightOS operating system.

Like Light's other technology, the phone was designed to be used as little as possible. It prioritises calling and is devoid of social media, games and other distractions.

Find out more about Light Flip ›

Robot Phone, by Honor

The Robot Phone by Honor features an articulating robot arm, which is topped with a gimbal-based 200-megapixel camera. It was designed to record more professional-looking video with pan and tilt functions that keep it level despite movement.

According to Honor, the robot arm will also help to form the basis for a more "human", expressive style of interaction with the phone, which was designed to incorporate new AI capabilities.

Find out more about Robot Phone ›

item.content:encoded:
US architecture studio KTGY has revamped the interiors of the HOK-designed Fairmont Hotel off of Chicago's Millennium Park.

KTGY's Interiors Studio was brought on to refresh the detailing and bring light into the dark spaces of the hotel, with a focus on the premium rooms and lounges. In total, the studio renovated 83 rooms, as well as meeting rooms and a terrace on the second level.

Originally designed by global studio HOK in the 1980s, the postmodern skyscraper hotel in Chicago's Millennium Park neighbourhood features a rationalised structure with neoclassical columns at the base. At the top, it's crowned by an oxidised copper turret that recalls the distinct châteauesque style of Fairmont hotels.

However, the elongated body gives the building a sense of verticality more akin to a modern skyscraper, with the mix of the historical and industrial contributing to the "postmodern" descriptions of the building.

The studio said that the primary reason behind the renovation was reflecting aspects of the postmodern skyscraper's facade in the interior, bringing the details down to scale.

"KTGY's interiors team reflected the building's postmodern architectural style by bringing that prominence down to a human scale," said the team.

Read:

Tatjana von Stein blends Jugendstil style with 1980s glamour for The Dean Munich

This included the uncovering of previously concealed architectural details, such as in the Rouge meeting room, where KTGY revealed windows and raised a sunken floor.

Here and throughout, the team integrated a visual palette that is modern while retaining some of the decadent detailing – such as an abstract chandelier and a textural sideboard, flanked by roped-LED sconces.

In the 15th-floor lounge, the studio completely redid the finishes and flooring and placed a library area to make the space feel more homey.

On the second-floor terrace, patterned wood flooring meets fluted wall details painted a matte green.

The rooms themselves were given lighter colours and bronze accents.

Fairmont Chicago Millennium Park is among the dozens of architectural landmarks in central Chicago. Nearby is Edward Durell Stone's AON Tower and Studio Gang's Aqua.

The photography is by Mike Schwartz.

item.content:encoded:
Brazil's Estúdio Campana has wrapped a pop-up Tiffany & Co store inside a São Paulo shopping mall in a woven wicker skin.

The pop-up on the ground floor of the JK Iguatemi Mall is cloaked in an undulating facade in Tiffany & Co's signature blue, with streaks of tan running horizontally across.

The collaboration with Estúdio Campana follows the studio's design for the brand's flagship store at another Iguatemi mall in São Paulo last year.

"After the success of the store at Shopping Iguatemi last year, we had the opportunity to reinterpret the original concept into a more intimate format, like a woven jewellery box that visitors can step into and immerse themselves in the brand's dreamlike universe," said Humberto Campana.

The long storefront is covered almost entirely in the wicker-style material, which parts to reveal the brand's illuminated logo mounted on beige stone.

Around an arched doorway that leads into the retail space, the blue wicker is folded over to house cove lighting that denotes the entrance.

The same facade treatment is also used at the back of the shop, forming another arch over a semi-private consultation area.

Blue tones are applied in swirling patterns to the seats and backs of chairs for customers, and across frames for wall-mounted mirrors.

Read:

MVRDV drapes glass veil around Tiffany & Co flagship in Beijing

Tiffany & Co products are presented in glass vitrines raised on metal-framed bases around tambour panelling.

Soft neutral tones were chosen for the remaining walls and carpet to contrast the bold blue elements, which feature in the brand's stores worldwide.

The studio created a chair and two mirrors from its Sushi Collection. It also fashioned a collection of custom synthetic-wicker stools, with manually woven elements that match the facade.

Recently, Tiffany & Co has worked with several notable architects and designers to update the facades of some of its global locations.

MVRDV draped a glass veil around the brand's Beijing flagship, while Jun Aoki cloaked a store in Ginza, Tokyo, in curving glass panels.

Estúdio Campana was founded by Humberto and his brother Fernando, who died in 2022. Humberto debuted his first design collection since his brother's passing at New York gallery Friedman Benda in 2024.

The studio has since created a park near São Paulo that includes pavilions made with live plants on land once farmed by the founders' grandfather.

The photography is courtesy of Iguatemi.

item.content:encoded:
Local studio Sordo Madaleno Arquitectos has completed the Arte Abierto Baja in Mexico, an open-air exhibition space wrapped by monolithic walls of exposed concrete and stone.

Designed for non-profit arts organisation Arte Abierto, the 180-square-metre space in the resort of Cabo del Sol is part of a wider masterplan by Sordo Madaleno Arquitectos for a retail development named Anima Village.

The Mexico City-based studio responded to the sloping site, which overlooks the sea at its eastern end, by partially sinking the gallery four metres below ground, where it is accessed via a long ramp flanked by rough stone walls.

At the gallery's centre, a cubic space is wrapped by five-metre-high concrete walls that block out everything except the sky and treetops, creating changing shadows throughout the day.

"We wanted a space that was open enough for art, nature, and community to converge in different ways each time," the studio's principal Fernando Sordo Madaleno told Dezeen.

"The open-air, below-grade configuration becomes a curatorial prompt – a conventional white cube closes the work in. Here, landscape, light, and sea breeze shape the viewing and making experience," he added.

Against the grid of Anima Village, the plan of Arte Abierto Baja has been rotated 45 degrees, with the entrance ramp leading into one of the square plan's corners.

At the base of this ramp, the stone walls continue to wrap the central concrete space, creating a darker corridor around the gallery's perimeter that is partially sheltered by a concrete roof.

Read:

Snøhetta adds reflective underground extension to Ordrupgaard Museum

Both a clockwise ramped route and an anticlockwise stepped route lead to an opening in the gallery's southwestern corner, where the darker corridor opens out into the brick exhibition area.

Drawing on the desert landscape of its surroundings, the floor of the exhibition space is covered in sandy soil, and the exposed concrete has been bush-hammered and pigmented a sandy shade to match.

"Descending into the gallery – by ramp or stair – you move out of the commercial activity above into something quieter: compressed, then opening, with light and sea breeze meeting the work," Madaleno said.

"The materials form part of the space's curatorial logic – sculpture and installations are set against an earthy backdrop and nature itself, mingling with shifting light and wind throughout the hours of the day," he added.

Other projects recently completed in Baja California include a mixed-use development by Barde vanVoltt, with a community cafe and residences finished in yellow-tinted plaster informed by the surrounding desert.

Another sunken gallery recently featured on Dezeen is an extension to Denmark's Ordrupgaard Museum by Snøhetta.

The photography is by Pablo Manjarrez.

item.content:encoded:
From outdoor courts that act as flood-water-draining bioswales to an indoor court under a concrete dome in Chile, here are seven basketball courts that integrate good design to expand their presence beyond the game.

Whether public or private, basketball courts present plenty of opportunities for distinguishing design elements.

This includes graphics laid out on the courts themselves, interesting support structures for hoops and even auxiliary design features, such as flood mitigation. One of the below is even dismountable, creating options for courts wherever one goes.

Read on for seven basketball courts that utilise fun and useful design strategies.

Sadler Close multi-use games area (MUGA), by POOR Collective, UK

Social enterprise POOR Collective worked with residents to renovate a multi-use court wedged into the corner of an estate in Mitcham, London.

Damaged basketball rims and surfacing were replaced using non-slip paint, with graphics that reference the patterns of the neighbouring tower blocks, while safety features such as lighting were added.

Find out more about Sadler Close MUGA ›

ALMA Sports Facility, by Benjamín Murúa Arquitectos, Chile 

Located at the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) Observatory in a remote desert location, this basketball court is part of a sports facility underground, topped at the surface by an assumed dome.

Framed by massive glulam trusses that conform to the dome's shape, the court in the facility allows researchers to exercise in all weather conditions, safely underground. It is heated by geothermal energy, which makes its energy consumption extremely low.

Find out more about ALMA Sports Facility ›

Huachiao Vibrant Sports Park, by SoBA Architects, China

A figurative design in Suzhou, this sports park was designed based on the "water sleeves" used in Kunqu operas, with meandering colourful paths set into the greenscaping.

Skatepark elements lead up to the two fenced-in basketball courts, with painted metal mesh fencing that aligns with the pastel colours of the courts.

Find out more about Huachiao Vibrant Sports Park ›

Idaho Central Credit Union Arena, by Opsis Architecture, USA

This court sits at the centre of an arena at the University of Idaho. The architecture studio wanted to depart from the typical concrete arena structures and use mass timber to host games and other functions.

The standard collegiate court sits under arcing spans of mass timber, while a number of auxiliary courts are located on the backsides of the bleachers.

Find out more about daho Central Credit Union Arena ›

 The City Is A Playground, by Eric Treillard, the Netherlands

Design Academy Eindhoven graduate Eric Treillard created a kit of parts that allows users to create a basketball court in unlikely places, with a hoop, ball, lights and a speaker, all of which can be packed onto a wheeled cart.

The hoop can be clamped with screws on top of walls, showing that courts can be set up anywhere.

Find out more about The City Is A Playground ›

Tompkins Square Park courts, by Na Chainkua Reindorf  for Glossier, USA

Beauty brand Glossier teamed up with the WNBA, the New York City Parks Department and non-profit Project Blackboard to restore this court, which saw artist Na Chainkua Reindorf sizing up her art style to cover its flooring.

The colourful design accompanied the resurfacing, providing a better playing surface while creating excitement for the neighbourhood.

Find out more about Tompkins Square Park courts ›

Water Square, by Grain Collective, USA

Located on a block managed by the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) in Queens, New York, this basketball court is the pilot in the city's Cloudburst programme to create bioswales to gather flood water.

The courts themselves were restored and sit above a drainage system that funnels flood water into basins that can hold hundreds of thousands of gallons, combining community amenities with water-management infrastructure.

Find out more about Water Square ›

item.content:encoded:
This week on Dezeen, IKEA shared a first look at its Konstrunda collection, which elevates "everyday objects into art pieces" with contributions from seven designers, including Andu Masebo and Lisa Hilland.

The 22-piece collection aims to offer an entry point for young collectors just beginning to accumulate pieces for their home, at prices they can actually afford.

"To make something that can be considered art, that can also be accessible is a really interesting challenge to consider," said London's Andu Masebo, who contributed a side table wrapped in a chunky metal frame.

In other design news, the first production model of Ferrari's first electric car – the opinion-dividing Ferrari Luce – sold for a record $40 million at a charity auction during Monterey Car Week in California.

Designed by Apple alumni Jony Ive and Marc Newson, the EV is now the most expensive new vehicle ever sold at auction, flying in the face of critics who argued that with four doors, five seats and zero engine, it wasn't a real Ferrari.

Also taking on records this week were architecture studios Waugh Thistleton Architects and Mithun, who unveiled their design for the "tallest mass timber office building in the US".

The 12-storey mass timber office block will be set in Bellevue, Washington, and demonstrates that "timber is ready to take its place at the forefront of American architecture" – at least according to Waugh Thistleton Architects co-founder Andrew Waugh.

Architecture firm OMA celebrated its own first this week, with the completion of its debut affordable housing development in the United States, set near Golden Gate Park in San Francisco.

We also revealed exclusive images of the new facade on the postmodern Thompson Center in downtown Chicago, installed as part of a renovation by architecture studio Jahn that will see it converted into Google's HQ in the Windy City.

Meanwhile, American actor Brad Pitt has taken on the role of executive producer for a documentary on Swiss architect Peter Zumthor, directed by German filmmaker Wim Wenders.

The 3D film, recorded over the course of 14 years, is set to premiere at the Venice Film Festival next month and aims to immerse audiences in the Pritzker Prize-winning architect's buildings.

Among our most popular projects this week are a concrete extension to a Lisbon school, the Chenhu Migratory Bird Observation Tower and a Norwegian cabin made from uprooted spruce trees.

item.content:encoded:
US food company Kraft Heinz has created an adjustable cap for its ketchup bottles that allows users to snap it into different positions to control the rate of flow.

The limited edition Love Lid was designed in collaboration with industrial design studio Beta Design Office and advertising agency Wieden+Kennedy London and works much like an adjustable hose nozzle.

The updated bottle looks similar to the current iteration, where the lid is located on the bottom and flips open for subsequent squeezing.

With the Love Lid, however, there are three settings labelled in red lettering – Like, Love, and Crazy Love.

Redesign celebrates users' "deeply personal rituals"

"The Heinz Love Lid is the first customizable ketchup lid designed to empower fans to choose their perfect squeeze of ketchup for summer's favorite foods," said the brand.

The rate of ketchup output adjusts with each setting and grows increasingly thick with each snap.

Read:

Heinz creates fry box with built-in ketchup compartment to "make dipping effortless"

According to the company, its creation was informed by a Reddit thread where commentators discussed how many bottles of Ketchup they use on average.

"People have deeply personal rituals around how much ketchup they squeeze, and we celebrate every one of them," said Global Heinz at the Kraft Heinz Company vice president Nina Patel.

"The Love Lid is an innovation that lets consumers squeeze to their heart's content, because Heinz has always been more than a condiment."

Limited-edition lid part of plan to expand Heinz' reach

The lid is a limited edition and follows in the company's more recent quest to evolve its packaging "to expand its reach while reinforcing fans' irrational love for its unmistakably rich sauce".

Heinz also released a fry box earlier this year with a built-in ketchup pocket for dipping.

"We all experience love differently and our fans' connection to ketchup is no exception," said Patel.

Heinz ketchup first went on sale in 1876 to US consumers. Today, according to The Economist, more than 650 million bottles are sold globally per year, with North America leading sales.

Other recent packaging design updates include a wrapper by KitKat that doubles as a smartphone pouch to put the devices "on a break" and packaging by Japanese snack food brand Calbee printed in black and white as a response to material shortages from the ongoing Iran war.

The image is courtesy of Kraft Heinz.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a proposal for a storehouse in Brent, UK, that keeps cultural artefacts is among the student projects from the London School of Architecture.

Also featured is a project that proposes "river rights" as a framework for rethinking our relationship with the natural world and a proposal for a housing community in Bethnal Green, London, which supports young carers.

London School of Architecture

School: London School of Architecture
Course: MArch Designing Architecture
Tutor: Ruth Lang

School Statement:

"The London School of Architecture (LSA) MArch programme unites a network of professional practitioners and academics to support a new generation of architects equipped and empowered to address real-world challenges, including the climate emergency and rampant inequity in urban life.

"Our 2026 degree show, If Only We Will, reinterprets the ideas and optimism central to the 1948 County of London Plan by John Henry Forshaw and Sir Leslie Patrick Abercrombie, using this as a critical point of reference through which to examine and situate student work in relation to current challenges across the sector.

"The projects presented here are grounded entirely within London, engaging directly with the city's social, environmental, political and spatial complexities.

"Collectively, they demonstrate how architecture can act as a vehicle for more equitable, healthy, sustainable and joyful ways of living.

"This year has been transformative for the LSA, highlighted by our merger with the University of the Built Environment.

"The work on display stands as a powerful provocation for what this future can hold – ambitious, socially engaged and attuned to the opportunities that emerge when disciplines intersect.

"Above all, our graduates demonstrate their capacity to reshape the context in which practice operates."

Architecture as a Framework for Care, Making and Transition by William Brooks

"The project focuses on care leavers – young people who are expected to become independent earlier than many of their peers, often without stable family, financial or emotional support.

"It proposes Hollybush Yard in Bethnal Green as a supported housing and learning community where independence is developed gradually through living, making and shared experience."

"Set within a historic builder's yard, the scheme draws on the site's legacy of construction, repair and material work.

"Rather than erasing this history, the project reactivates it through workshops, shared yards, co-living spaces and learning environments."

Student: William Brooks
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

Maker Commons by Thomas Simms

"Situated within Hackney Wick and Fish Island, Maker Commons responds to the gradual displacement of industrial spaces, creative networks and productive communities through cycles of redevelopment following the Olympic Games.

"It investigates how architecture can re-establish these shared infrastructures for material production within urban areas shaped by regeneration-led development.

"While creativity remains central to the area's identity, it has increasingly been aestheticised and repackaged as a cultural asset in support of investor-led growth.

"The project proposes a new form of urban commons that repositions making, repair and skill-sharing as visible and essential civic activities rather than temporary uses."

Student: Thomas Simms
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

What Would the Modern Day City Look Like if Rivers Had Rights? by Elen Togher

"The project is situated within the context of the current climate and ecological crises and proposes river rights as a framework for rethinking our relationship with the natural world.

"Rather than treating rivers as resources to be controlled and exploited, the project explores how recognising rivers as rights-bearing entities could be a stepping stone towards environmental stability.

"Situated along the River Lea, the project proposes an extensive reed filtration network, lido house and river parliament, providing space for river recreation, immersion and representation.

"Constructed from materials of the riverscape, the architecture is intentionally impermanent whilst the landscape heals itself over time."

Student: Elen Togher
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

Time and Tide: Unearthing Resilience on the City of London's North Bank by Josie Tindale

"Time and Tide reimagines London's relationship with the River Thames to respond to the projected failure of the Thames Barrier.

"The proposal integrates flood-resilient infrastructure into the City of London's North Bank; unearthing ancient archaeology to enhance heritage, support biodiversity and shape public spaces.

"The excavated material is reused in a tangible celebration of traditional Roman/Medieval construction.

"Drawing on the city's historic connection to the Thames, the scheme seeks to 'soften the edge' of the river following centuries of hard embankment.

"The heart of the scheme is a space for London where history, water, ecology and public life coexist."

Student: Josie Tindale
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

Feeding Kilburn by Rachel Opie

"This thesis investigates how architecture can intervene before demolition to enable new forms of community-led civic infrastructure.

"Challenging conventional models of regeneration that rely on clearance and replacement, this project proposes deconstruction as a design process, where buildings are carefully dismantled to recover materials and spatial potential.

"These elements are then reassembled through strategies of adaptive reuse to form frameworks that support evolving forms of occupation.

"By working with what already exists, rather than erasing it, the thesis positions material reuse as a spatial and social strategy for sustaining community presence and agency within the changing city."

Student: Rachel Opie
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

Ephemeral Boundaries: Adaptive Reuse as a Pedagogy of Curiosity and Movement by Gloria Hii

"Schools are under pressure to do more than teach. In a post-Covid context, they are expected to support wellbeing, care and social recovery, yet many continue to operate within ageing buildings, rigid classrooms and regulated indoor environments.

"In London, fresh ventilation falters within a culture of standardised comfort, where climate is controlled, sealed and regulated. As a result, curiosity, autonomy and sensory engagement can become suppressed.

"Ephemeral Boundaries argues for an adaptive educational environment that restores school as a porous civic infrastructure, where fresh air is understood not only as a technical requirement, but as a spatial and pedagogical experience."

Student: Gloria Hii
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

Designing for Mental Health by Sam Wimbush

"This project began with a seemingly simple question: how can architecture better support mental health?

"Drawing from personal experiences of the NHS mental health system, conversations with service users and wider research into contemporary healthcare provision, it quickly became apparent that the challenges extend far beyond the design of individual buildings.

"Rather than concentrating services within large institutional campuses, care is distributed through a network of familiar and accessible spaces, including community businesses, enhanced GP facilities, therapeutic environments and short-stay accommodation providing support before crisis occurs."

Student: Sam Wimbush
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

Unplanning Suburbia: Unlocking An Alternative Future For London's Metroland by Caspar Barker

"With London's population projected to grow to over 11 million by 2050, when London's remaining major brownfield development sites will have all been completed, alternative approaches to building new homes in the capital are going to be required.

"My thesis stands in direct opposition to the Labour government's 2024 planning reforms to permit development on select greenbelt land, and instead I would like to confront how planning reform might bring opportunities for mutually beneficial development among London's vast low-density suburban neighbourhoods to counter urban sprawl."

Student: Caspar Barker
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

Common'ing The Boundary by Alex Handy

"The project is a response to the question: What if a neighbourhood could retrofit itself? It proposes an alternative model for the retrofit of UK social housing estates, repositioning retrofit as a collective, materially grounded, and locally embedded process."

"Using the Boundary Estate in London as a test site, the project explores how housing estates can become productive landscapes capable of generating the materials, skills, and governance structures required for their own retrofit.

"The proposal challenges top-down models of retrofit delivery and presents a transferable model for the decentralised retrofit of urban housing across London."

Student: Alex Handy
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

New Imaginaries of Resistance in the Suburban Ends by Anu Sofuyi

"Located in Preston, a suburb in Brent, this thesis proposes a storehouse for cultural artefacts and processes beyond objects: an ever-evolving reflection of diasporic activity.

"It makes the case for a new suburban imagination that seeks to make visible the invisible, and in doing so celebrates the past, present, and future of communal cultural production by the Suburban Mandem.

"Adopting a methodology of speculative fiction using 'hood futurism' (Nabil Al-Kinani, 2024) as a theoretical lens, the project consists of a set of interventions made up of three threads – broadcasting, service and distribution."

Student: Anu Sofuyi
Course: MArch Designing Architecture

Partnership content

item.content:encoded:
Toronto architecture studio UUfie has expanded and renovated a 1970s chalet in Ontario to conform to its steep, wooded site with a net that serves as an internal barrier and a hammock.

Set on 3 acres within the Niagara Escarpment, Belfountain House preserves the northern portion of the original structure, while transforming the southern half within the existing footprint. A single, elongated roof gathers the two portions under a span that follows the slope of the site.

"We were interested in how the house could feel less like an object placed on the land and more like something shaped by it," UUfie cofounder Irene Gardpoit told Dezeen.

"This led us to think sectionally from the beginning – to work with the slope and the changing ground conditions rather than against them."

The resulting 430-square-metre (4,628-square-foot) house has four storeys within a 238-square-metre (2,561-square-foot) footprint and is organised based on the circulation up and down the slope.

"We imagined the experience almost like a hike, where spaces unfold through gradual transitions, changing views and moments of pause," cofounder Eiri Ota said.

"More than anything, the goal was to create a home that feels embedded in the landscape and responsive to the way a family actually lives."

From the outside, the house is a series of white stucco and black wood shapes connected by black metal balcony railings, roof lines and window frames surrounding glazing that reveals the unusual angles of the interior.

Inside, the spaces function as a continuous landscape, rather than a set of enclosed rooms.

The upper side of the house gathers bedrooms and family spaces – kitchen, dining and living rooms – under a gable with duelling staircases, while the lower side cascades down the hillside with open tiers of spaces.

A suspended net divides the dining and lounge spaces from the hallway and recreation room below, serving as both a barrier and a hammock.

"[The net] is not only functional, but also transforms the experience of the sectional volume by introducing porosity, playfulness and transparency," the studio said.

The landing level between the upper and lower features a sauna and gym.

At the lowest point of the site, a well-like structure with a steeply vaulted ceiling and a skylight serves as a guest room.

Read:

UUfie completes light-filled Ontario medical clinic with translucent polycarbonate walls

The sloped wall that separates the suite from the house above is made of polycarbonate that filters and diffuses light, giving the room a softer, luminous atmosphere.

"The material palette was developed to create a balance between softness and ruggedness, refinement and rawness," the studio said, pointing out rich reclaimed elm and radiant concrete floors with large aggregate.

"By contrast, the red steel beams add a sharper, more graphic note, creating a strong diagonal counterpoint to the wood rafters."

Founded in Tokyo in 2009 and based in Toronto since 2013, UUfie designs furniture, installation and architecture across residential, cultural and commercial markets.

Previously, the studio completed an Ontario medical clinic with polycarbonate walls, a Shanghai boutique with a pixelated glass facade and a Canadian lakeside cottage with a mirrored entrance.

item.content:encoded:
A crisp white cube has been nested within the old brick shell of an existing building to create Casa Nido, a Spanish house designed by local studio Iterare Arquitectos.

Casa Nido, or Nesting House, was designed to highlight an example of the relatively scarce architectural heritage in the northern neighbourhood of Torrefiel in Valencia, on a site flanked by taller residential blocks.

Iterare Arquitectos designed the intervention to be deliberately "brutal" and pared-back, finishing both its exterior and interior in crisp white render and limestone to throw the existing rough brickwork into relief.

"The existing building was not an extraordinary piece of architecture, nor was it a monument of any kind; yet for us, it represented a very distinct fragment of memory that had survived radical changes in the area," the studio's co-founder Rubén Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

"We decided to be brutal about it," added Gutiérrez. "We completely stripped the plaster covering the brickwork, repaired the masonry and its mortar, and sealed the openings we didn’t need while leaving their outlines visible to record the building's history prior to our intervention."

"It is very important to note that this was only possible because neither the building nor the area had any heritage protection status, allowing us the freedom to intervene, or even demolish and build anew, had we chosen to," he continued.

Facing the street corner, the exterior of the home has been left largely blank, with its existing openings either filled with concrete or small windows that have white limestone louvres to offer privacy to the bedroom and bathroom.

This almost windowless exterior is enabled by a large paved patio at the back of the site, onto which a double-height living, dining and kitchen space opens via folding doors within a fully-glazed wall.

Read:

The Parchment Works house extension built inside ruined stone walls

High, white walls wrap this patio, reflecting soft light deep into the dining and kitchen area, which has also been finished with limestone floors, white walls and ceilings.

A timber staircase leads up to a mezzanine containing the more intimate living space, which is illuminated by a thin skylight along the opposite edge of the home.

"The courtyard occupies one-third of the site, but more importantly, it represents one-third of the overall interior volume," Gutiérrez explained.

"The entire interior projects toward this courtyard – or more precisely, the whole inner volume is sheltered, protected, and enclosed by the same perimeter walls. This creates a powerful sense of protection and calmness," he added.

Previous projects by Iterare Arquitectos include another renovation in Valencia, which used a minimal palette of traditional materials to update a 100-year-old home.

Another home built within the shell of another building is The Parchment Works by Will Gamble Architects. The house incorporates the ruins of a 17th-century parchment factory and an old cattle shed.

The photography is by David Zarzoso.

item.content:encoded:
Photographer Ahmad Alnaji has captured the Ciel Dubai Marina, a supertall skyscraper by architecture studio NORR that was recently completed as the tallest hotel in the world.

Ciel Dubai Marina opened in November last year, rising 377 metres to beat the 356-metre-tall Gevora Hotel, also in Dubai, as the world's tallest hotel-only building.

Alnaji, founder of photography studio Sarab, was commissioned by NORR project lead Yahya Jan to capture the Ciel Dubai Marina as the architect "intended it to be seen".

"Jan wanted photos that are artistic yet don't deceive the viewer about the true design and elements of Ciel," Alnaji told Dezeen. "The photos are made to tell the story of a unique architectural icon."

Operated by IHG's Vignette Collection hotels, Ciel Dubai Marina contains 1,004 hotel rooms, eight cafes and restaurants, a spa, gym, and amenities for children.

Built atop a white-clad podium, the skyscraper has a tapering form that narrows at the top and bottom, with curved facades clad in cold-bent glass panels designed to reflect prevailing winds.

Read:

Ten record-breaking skyscrapers from around the world

Evocative of the eye of a needle, an opening in the upper portion of the 82-storey skyscraper contains an infinity pool on the 76th floor overlooking the surrounding Dubai Marina.

The opening is bridged above by a publicly accessible observation deck, while below, a 300-metre-tall atrium split into a series of terraces forms the spine of the skyscraper.

"Inside, the architecture centres on a 300-metre atrium cut through the tower's core, holding vertically stacked, landscaped sky gardens with naturally ventilated terraces spaced through the height of the building," said Alnaji

"These are Jan's answer to vertical living, daylit communal voids that bring planting and shared space into a supertall hotel rather than stacking rooms alone."

Founded in 1938, NORR is an architecture, engineering and planning studio with offices in cities across Canada, the USA and the UK.

Other towering buildings that are set to be built in Dubai, a place famed for its skyscraper-heavy skyline, include a Mercedes-Benz-branded series of residential skyscrapers and MVRDV's plans for a skyscraper with a giant orb on its upper floors.

The photography is by Ahmad Alnaji.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio ZHA has unveiled its masterplan for Baku Expo City in Azerbaijan, where overlapping stacked homes with green roofs will flank an extension to the city's exhibition centre.

The 198-hectare-site in Baku will have residences ranging from one-bedroom flats to larger family homes. ZHA's masterplan also includes civic institutions and cultural venues, as well as public parks, medical clinics and sports clubs.

A new Baku Expo Center extension and Congress Hall will be at the centre of the masterplan, in an area that will also feature a hotel and a public square with leisure and hospitality venues.

Renderings of the residences show stacked white buildings with blocky geometric shapes, designed as interconnected neighbourhoods where houses overlap one another.

The building layout was designed so that some houses would serve as protective barriers against harsh winds. ZHA also used pedestrian wind-comfort analysis to reduce wind speeds and create sheltered public spaces.

This is because Baku, known as the City of Winds, experiences both the Khazri wind in winter and the Gilavar wind in summer.

Read:

Heydar Aliyev Centre is the ultimate expression of parametricism's "seamless fluidity"

The homes will be nestled in an existing pine tree forest, and according to ZHA, the masterplan will preserve 80 per cent of the 18,000 trees on the site.

To make sure the forest continues to mature, the design also incorporates forestry management, while green roofs on all the houses will help the buildings blend into the site. A replanting programme has also been included in the masterplan.

ZHA said that the green roofs will help to reduce cooling energy demand and enhance thermal insulation, while functioning as an integral part of the site's rainwater collection system.

"The masterplan prioritises a sustainable, people-centred environment by integrating renewable solar and wind energy, passive design strategies, effective water management and low-carbon material choices," the studio said.

"These measures create highly efficient residential and civic infrastructure together with comfortable outdoor spaces within a vibrant, resilient community that supports the long-term ecological health of the city."

Public transport, including the upgraded Bakikhanov-Bina-Gala rail line, will connect Baku Expo City to the Baku city centre and airport.

ZHA has previously designed the parametricist Heydar Aliyev Centre in Baku, while the city's international airport was created by Turkish studio Autoban.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles studio Waka Waka has designed Ribbon, an undulating furniture collection made from steel and aluminium decorated with saturated colours, for Japanese manufacturer Benex's Eetal project.

Eetal, which presented a selection of sheet-metal furniture during design festival 3 Days of Design in Copenhagen this year, commissions designers to find uses for Benex's aluminium and steel sheets.

For Waka Waka, which normally works with plywood, it was an opportunity to expand on the studio's previous work.

"I primarily use Baltic birch plywood at our studio as our signature material," Waka Waka designer Shinichiro Okuda told Dezeen. "For this collaboration, I wanted to explore the design possibilities of metal, but specifically using a sheet material as I approach plywood."

The Ribbon collection comprises a chair, a table and a stool in different colours, as well as smaller accessories, including a tray, a clothes hanger and two different clothes racks.

All of the pieces were designed using simple geometric shapes, such as circles, squares and arches, and feature details including ribbon-like glossy, folded edges.

"Metal gives a feeling of coolness, structure, and sometimes confinement," Okuda said.

"The ribbon was a way to create a fluid line quality, imparting warmth and a sense of nature. Also, we wanted to accentuate the qualities of the material rather than mask or hide them."

Waka Waka also wanted the pieces to have an industrial feel to underline the inherent qualities of the aluminium and steel used for the furniture.

"Referencing industrial colours, hardware and connection points was intentional to present the metal as metal, not as a substitute for plywood," Okuda said.

The Ribbon pieces come in colours including yellow, pink and black, as well as a blue hue that Okuda says was chosen after the studio came across it when visiting a Benex factory.

"We picked the first colour, blue, after noticing it during our first factory visit," he said.

Read:

Seven exhibitions that showcased Japanese design in Copenhagen

"The blue was one of the existing standard factory colours used for many industrial products they manufacture, and it is a blue specific to Japan," Okuda continued.

"I still wanted to accentuate the materiality of the metal, so this industrial blue felt very fitting."

To match the blue colour, Okuda chose hues from Japan's prosperous Edo period.

"We picked other colour combinations from the Edo period," he said. "The saturated colours are pairings that feel both recognisable and livable."

Overall, Waka Waka aimed to give the cold metal material a warmer feel.

"Metal gives a feeling of coolness, structure, and sometimes confinement," Okuda said. "The ribbon was a way to create a fluid line quality, imparting warmth and a sense of nature."

The Ribbon collection has been shown in its own exhibition in Tokyo and Osaka and will be presented in Los Angeles in September, followed by exhibitions in Fukuoka and Nagasaki.

Another metal design recently featured on Dezeen is a Dieter Rams door handle that was redesigned in an all-metal version.

The photography is by Kenta Hasegawa.

Ribbon will be shown at Small Office, 3465 Casitas Avenue, Los Angeles, California, from September 12 to 27. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: according to software company Chaos, AI-assisted tools, advances in rendering technologies, and shifting client expectations are transforming the architecture industry's visualisation workflows into a flexible communication tool.

Chaos explained that utilising artificial intelligence has enabled visualisation to evolve into a valuable communication aid, which supports the creative process from early concept development through to final presentation.

"Visualisation is no longer a single visual output delivered at the end of the process," said Chaos.

"As photorealistic imagery becomes the new standard in an increasingly artificial intelligence-driven era, the ability to create meaningful emotional narratives is emerging as the real differentiator," it added.

According to Chaos, this shift in how visualisations are being used is due to client expectations and the need for a quicker, more flexible workflow.

Chaos explained that instead of starting a project from scratch, architects and designers now often begin projects by reacting to AI-generated moodboards or concepts provided by the client.

This flexibility speeds up the workflow process by bridging the gap between a client's "AI dream" and a professional, buildable reality.

"AI-powered tools save hours of manual refinement"

The company added that AI-powered visualisation tools also enable creatives to better connect their early ideas to final designs while minimising time spent on time-consuming tasks.

Specifically, Chaos believes the tools can streamline the early design process involving testing ideas before committing to a design, as well as taking on the time-consuming task of final visuals for a client.

"Repetitive manual work remains common in visualisation tasks, from refining textures and correcting lighting noise to improving image clarity and preparing images for final delivery," said Chaos. "AI-powered tools are increasingly helping to automate these steps, saving hours of manual refinement."

"Acting as a brainstorming partner in the early stage of the design process, AI-assisted tools make it possible to generate ideas without spending hours on rendering and testing different prototypes without fully building a project," added the company.

AI is a "storytelling tool"

According to Chaos, visualisation should not only be seen as a tool to illustrate final designs, but also as a "storytelling tool".

"Artificial intelligence is becoming an essential part of the architectural visualisation workflow," Chaos explained. "Rather than replacing creative decision-making, AI-assisted tools are helping professionals focus on storytelling."

Chaos also explained that another benefit of incorporating AI ideation is that it enables more efficient workflows, not only at the beginning but throughout the whole design process.

"Switching between multiple tools and fragmented workflows places a significant burden on anyone managing complex projects," said Chaos.

"By embracing a hybrid workflow, designers can combine real-time tools for instant feedback with high-quality photorealistic imagery for marketing materials and final approvals," it continued.

"The transition from linear to a hybrid workflow is ultimately a creative win. By reducing friction throughout the process, professionals can move beyond technical constraints and focus on what truly sets their work apart: emotional storytelling."

To learn more about AI-assisted visualisation workflows, visit Chaos' website.

The visuals are courtesy of Chaos.

item.content:encoded:
A team including Studio Barnes and Ch_studio has revealed designs to transform the 1920s building once used by the white supremacist group the Ku Klux Klan in Fort Worth, Texas, into a "catalyst for community and restoration".

The 35,000-square-foot (3,251 square metre) building is located between Fort Worth's Historic Northside and downtown area, and its planned transformation will be an act of "reparative justice" according to its design team.

The Transform 1012 Center for Arts and Community Healing building will contain three levels with programming dedicated to local cultural and arts groups, including a theatre, makerspaces, classrooms, dance spaces, a bar and cafe and an outdoor amphitheatre.

The building was once a base of Ku Klux Klan (KKK) activity before the group vacated the property in 1927. It was then bought by a local department store and later held the Ellis Pecan Company between 1946 and 1999.

The adaptive reuse design by architecture offices Studio Barnes, Ch_studio and GFF with landscape architecture practice JIMA Studio "seeks to confront the past rather than erase it" and centres around a balance of preserving historical elements, such as the brick facade, while introducing contemporary elements, such as reorganising the interior.

"For us, the central challenge was determining how to transform a structure defined by racial violence into a catalyst for community and restoration," said the design team in a joint statement.

"While the site's dark history offered a strong case for tearing down the structure, our design approach seeks to confront the past rather than erase it."

In particular, the group sought to open up the interior and exterior to new sightlines and passageways that cut through the entirety of the site to contrast the former design building to "intimidate and divide".

Renderings show the new building clad in its original brick facade interspersed with other textures and materials such as weathering steel, striated concrete panels, and perforated metal screens.

Openings, plazas, curving pathways and a lush landscape are also shown throughout the property.

The building's programming will be dedicated to groups that have suffered from the KKK's violence and exclusion, according to the team, including Black, Catholic, Hispanic, immigrant, Jewish, and LGBTQ+ communities.

The project has been led by local group Transform 1012 N Main Street, a coalition including parties such as SOL Ballet Folklórico, The Welman Project and activist Dr Opal Lee, which purchased the building in 2021.

Read:

Lake Flato plans to create "vibrant, mixed-use waterfront district" on Fort Worth island

A second-floor gallery will also be dedicated to the histories of race relations in North Texas and highlight the memory of Fred Rouse, a Black father and butcher lynched in Fort Worth in 1921.

The building's landscape will include design based on African Diasporic, Indigenous, and Mexican Diasporic traditions.

The team seeks to reuse waste materials, and according to the team, has already diverted more than 195 tons of material from landfills, including concrete and lumber, for the build.

Construction is anticipated to begin in Summer 2027, with opening slated for Winter 2028.

The KKK was founded in the late 1860s in Tennessee. Throughout the decades, it has operated in both secrecy and flagrant displays of violence and racism, primarily against the Black community.

Although KKK activity has decreased since its founding, the group is still active around the US and elsewhere.

Other recent projects that seek to address the history of racial and discriminatory violence in the United States include the International African American Museum designed by Pei Cobb Freed & Partners and Moody Nolan and a Holocaust memorial in Florida.

The images are courtesy of Transform 1012 N Main Street.
