item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a project aiming to optimise architect Berthold Lubetkin's Grade I-listed Finsbury Health Centre for 21st-century users is among those by the University of Nottingham.

Also included are a scheme for a sustainability-centric primary school to encourage eco-conscious habits in children, and an urban regeneration plan for a historic high street in Norwich, UK.

University of Nottingham

Institution: University of Nottingham
School: Department of Architecture and Built Environment
Courses: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2), L7 Apprenticeship, MArch Sustainable Urban Design, MArch Advanced Architecture Design, and MArch Architecture and Sustainable Design
Tutors: Graeme Barker, Tim Collett, Amy Tang, Tim Heath, Lorna Kiamba, Renata Tubelo and Lucelia Rodrigues

School statement:

"The Department of Architecture and Built Environment at the University of Nottingham is a leading centre for education and research, preparing future architects, engineers and built-environment professionals to address global challenges.

"Building on a strong reputation for sustainability and innovation, the department offers a range of postgraduate programmes spanning architecture, sustainable design, environmental engineering, building performance and urban development.

"These combine academic excellence with practical application, equipping students with advanced technical expertise, problem-solving skills and a strong foundation in sustainability, as illustrated in the examples below.

"MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2) gives students the skills to become successful and employable architects. It is shaped around six core themes: sustainability, continuity, construction, urban transformation, social inclusivity, and inhabitation.

"MArch Sustainable Urban Design equips students with the design, research, and strategic planning skills needed to create sustainable, resilient and inclusive urban environments.

"MArch Advanced Architecture Design enables students to pursue contemporary agendas that address critical challenges within the built environment from a research-led design perspective.

"MArch Architecture and Sustainable Design integrates architecture with environmental performance and sustainable technologies, equipping students with design skills that respond to contemporary challenges."

Unbuilding Trent Basin: A Circular Resource Hub by Anthony Tse

"Unbuilding Trent Basin reimagines the existing city as a material repository rather than a landscape of obsolete structures.

"By transforming redundant warehouses into centres for urban mining, material exchange and collective making, the project treats the city itself as a resource bank rather than a site of continual extraction and replacement.

"Land liberated from storage and waste functions is gradually returned to productive landscapes, while reclaimed materials are recirculated into future construction.

"As a prototype for degrowth urbanism, the project challenges expansion-led development and demonstrates how cities can prosper through repair, reuse, and collective care."

Student: Anthony Tse
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Alison Davies and Richard Woods
Email: anthonytse98[at]gmail.com

City Commoning by Bethany Humphrey

"High street decline is an existential threat to communities in urban centres, who rely on them as critical social infrastructure ecosystems.

"This design includes a series of retrofits to vacant commercial units, temporary pavilions, and a green street pedestrianisation strategy along Norwich's historic Magdalen Street, an ecosystem at risk of being overwhelmed by residential expansion.

"These include a redundant medieval church adapted into a young enterprise hub, a former antiques emporium transformed into a youth centre, and a prefabricated market under St Crispin's Flyover.

"The social capital of the whole is greater than the sum of each space."

Student: Bethany Humphrey
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Tim Collett and Naomi Eckworth
Email: b.humphrey01[at]gmail.com

Architecture and Energy: A Self-Sustaining Sports Complex by Cecil Pun

"The thesis explores sustainability through the relationship between architecture and energy, informed by the theory of 'form follows fuel' – the idea that architectural form is shaped by dominant energy systems available to society.

"As we transition towards decarbonisation, the form must also evolve. The project reimagines Greenwich Power Station, a product of fossil fuel, as a self-sustaining sports complex that generates, stores, and conserves its own energy.

"Its environmental strategy prioritises passive design, renewable energy, and adaptable spaces that respond to seasonal change, reducing energy demand while reconnecting occupants with natural environmental conditions."

Student: Cecil Pun
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Tim Collett and Naomi Eckworth
Email: cecilpun[at]gmail.com

Tooting Exchange: Architecture Beyond Consumption by Emily Gibson

"Tooting Exchange offers a civic alternative to the contemporary high street.

"Set within the dense commercial fabric of Tooting Market, the project turns underused space into a setting for everyday participation, repair, learning and exchange.

"Instead of adding another consumption driven destination, it creates a porous social landscape that encourages lingering, gathering and informal occupation.

"Existing structures are kept and adapted over time, reducing embodied carbon while preserving the site's memory and identity.

"The project explores how architecture can give spatial form to principles of degrowth, sufficiency, conviviality, participation and collective wellbeing through adaptable civic infrastructure woven into the rhythms of the high street."

Student: Emily Gibson
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2) Level 7 Apprenticeship
Tutors: Nick Haynes and Paula Schilliger
Email: emily-gibson10[at]hotmail.co.uk

Agency of the Void: Between Institution and City by Evlin Servis

"Exploring how architecture can reconnect institutions with public life, the thesis proposes a hybrid civic-cultural institution on a residual wharf in Bristol, positioned between St Mary Redcliffe and the Floating Harbour.

"The scheme acts as a civic centre and extension to Bristol's existing Urban Room, using overlapping public interiors and layered thresholds to draw movement through the site, re-intensify the route between the city and St Mary Redcliffe and create a more legible and inhabitable public landscape.

"Through a pedestrianised urban realm, activated canal frontage and public cut-throughs, the scheme establishes a new urban promenade reconnecting communities and supporting regeneration."

Student: Evlin Servis
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Alison Davies and Richard Woods
Email: evlinservis[at]gmail.com

ReSource by Matthew James

"The architectural profession today finds itself at the intersection between two revolutions: a digital revolution threatening the agency of the maker, and an environmental one demanding a shift in our attitude toward material consumption.

"ReSource investigates the paradox between craftsmanship and circularity through the transformation of the soon-to-be-demolished Colechurch House, unlocking the huge material potential of an unloved building.

"This model exhibits 'Connective Craft' – part of the existing building is transformed: an extension structure is formed with steel from an existing bridge, removed concrete is stacked to form columns, and the precast cladding is rotated to create new shading."

Student: Matthew James
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Kate Nicklin and Graham Mateer
Email: matthew.t.james.studio[at]gmail.com

Catalyst Works by Oliver Roberts

"The Catalyst Works is an urban quarry for recovering, processing and redistributing architectural materials within the regeneration of Frog Island, Leicester.

"With regeneration understood as a time dependent process, the project is structured through three strategies – Permanence, Adaptability and Temporary Activation – allowing regeneration to occur incrementally through phased occupation and evolving use.

"Permanent interventions preserve embodied value and establish civic infrastructure, adaptable systems support long-term change, and temporary interventions catalyse early occupation and material reuse.

"Together, these strategies demonstrate how architecture can enable resilient, low-impact regeneration through circular material flows and incremental transformation."

Student: Oliver Roberts
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2)
Tutors: Kate Nicklin and Graham Mateer
Email: oj.roberts[at]yahoo.com

The Learning Grove by Gopika Pillai Deepu

"This sustainable primary school reimagines learning by shaping spaces that inspire children to discover, play and grow.

"The building is designed to reduce carbon emissions and encourage eco-conscious habits through solar integration, green mobility and creating environmental awareness.

"The design was supported by evidence-based tools such as IESVE, PHPP and Sefaira, ensuring strong environmental performance.

"Guided by RIBA sustainable outcomes, every space enhances daylight, air quality, and thermal comfort while maintaining a close connection to nature.

"Inclusive, accessible, and energy-efficient, the school becomes a living classroom where children learn to live lightly and grow toward a greener future."

Student: Gopika Pillai Deepu
Course: MArch Architecture and Sustainable Design
Tutors: Lorna Kiamba and Renata Tubelo
Email: ar.gopikapillai01[at]gmail.com

Therme Hill by Mithilesh Rani

"Therme Hill answers the question 'what if nature shaped urban health?' by anchoring memory, wellness and the vitality of living beside a 'hill', within a tropical wellness precinct.

"Situated along the quiet edge of the Bridgewater Canal in Trafford Park, the design counters industrial zoning and a harsh microclimate by enclosing a warm, tropical sanctuary beneath a monumental free-form grid shell while extending Manchester's green belt with a dense plantation.

"Integrating stalactite-inspired structural columns, suspended vegetation, family pools, an indoor beach and community farming, the project vitalises social sustainability by catalysing public access to nature in the city."

Student: Mithilesh Rani
Course: MArch Advanced Architecture Design
Tutors: Amy Tang, Tim Heath and Anran Chen
Email: laxmr10[at]nottingham.ac.uk

Reimagining Finsbury Health Centre: Architecture for Health by Aidan Sinclair

"This thesis reimagines the Grade I listed Finsbury Health Centre, extending Berthold Lubetkin's vision of public welfare for the 21st century.

"Rooted in the building's original commitment to collective wellbeing, the proposal transforms the site into a contemporary health and wellbeing district.

"Alongside primary healthcare services, the scheme introduces community programmes, exhibition spaces, and improved public realm.

"New civic spaces strengthen connections between local institutions, integrating healthcare, culture, and every day public life to reduce the stigma of accessing health services.

"Adaptive reuse preserves its heritage and supports future healthcare needs, demonstrating architecture's role in promoting public health and community cohesion."

Student: Aidan Sinclair
Course: MArch Architecture (ARB/RIBA Part 2) Level 7 Apprenticeship
Tutors: Nick Haynes and Paula Schilliger
Email: aidan_sinclair[at]outlook.com

item.content:encoded:
A brick cube reminiscent of old industrial structures forms this family home in the suburbs of Ghent, designed by Belgian architecture studio Atelier Vens Vanbelle.

Named Project Tomas & Katrien after its clients, but nicknamed The Factory by its neighbours, the cubic brick home was disguised as an industrial structure to help create the impression that it had "always been there", the studio said.

"We proposed to the city services to build our home against a large blind wall on the property boundary to neatly close off the row of houses, but the city did not want to go along with this idea," Atelier Vens Vanbelle told Dezeen.

"We were required to build a detached house. Therefore, we chose to design a brick building that refers to old industrial or workshop architecture, so that it creates the impression of having always been there."

Project Tomas & Katrien comprises two storeys organised around a central diamond-shaped skylight and light well, which features a lush green planter at its base and is traversed via a bright yellow staircase.

The beams of the home's ground-floor ceiling, as well as its paved and timber-plank floors, have all been positioned to align with this central void, setting them at diagonals to the edges of the home.

This 45-degree angle was also the basis of a diagonal wall on the ground floor that separates the large living, dining and kitchen area from a series of smaller service areas.

Upstairs, the home's four bedrooms are organised around a cross-shaped, multipurpose area that was designed to feel like an extension of the living area below, which it overlooks from behind a bright yellow balustrade.

Read:

Bricolage uses salvaged bricks for self-build home in London

"We wanted to avoid building a traditional home with a living area on the ground floor and an upper floor where there is hardly anything to do. We chose to build a home that can be experienced across both floors," the studio said.

"The 45-degree angle in the floor plan creates a captivating perspective, making the spaces feel even larger than they actually are."

"The materials evoke the atmosphere of an old workshop – bricks combined with old clay tiles, wooden walls and ceilings, and metal stairs and balustrades," added Atelier Vens Vanbelle.

"The palette is raw, yet feels homely and familiar at the same time."

At the end of the home's garden, a garden store is flanked by a bike shelter and seating area. It features perforated brick walls and is covered by a raised, sloping timber and polycarbonate roof.

Elsewhere in Ghent, local architecture studios Atelier Avondzon and Macadam Atelier also looked to industrial structures for their renovation of a derelict home, which features a sawtooth roof and corrugated metal cladding, while Decancq Vercruysse recently reorganised a mid-century bungalow around a fireplace.

The photography is courtesy of Atelier Vens Vanbelle.

item.content:encoded:
The Barbican Centre shop has launched a homeware collection with online retailer Made.com, which includes furniture and lighting modelled on details of the brutalist housing complex in central London.

Geometric, gridded and curved architectural references feature throughout the 23-piece MADE x Barbican homeware collection, which also includes textiles and accessories.

According to the Barbican, the collection was developed following research into the original Barbican Estate apartment layouts, including the work of designer Miriam Howitt, who created five show homes for the estate in the 1960s.

The pieces are designed to be used together or independently and prices start from £32.

"The ambition was to create a complete product range that works both in isolation and together in an open living space," said the Made.com team.

"The final designs reimagine products, graphics and architectural details through a new lens, and into a cohesive product range that captures Barbican living: bold, considered and inherently social."

The Barbican Estate was designed by Chamberlin, Powell and Bon in the 1950s and opened in 1982. It is one of the largest examples of post-war brutalist architecture in the UK.

Within it is the Barbican Centre – an arts and culture venue with theatres, galleries, cinemas, as well as a conservatory, a library and eateries.

A pair of stand-out pieces in the collection is the Curve Table Lamp and Curve Floor Lamp, which have adjustable, tubular shades that draw on the acoustic panels in the Barbican's concert hall.

The lights have chrome bases, with shades available in burgundy, green and blue, contrasted by their fabric cables.

Other lighting pieces include the Coffer ceiling lights and wall lights, which mimic the estate's iconic waffle ceilings, seen throughout its indoor and outdoor spaces.

Furniture pieces in the range include the Dual chairs, with statement side panels made of wood and modelled on the estate's concrete pillars, and the modular Plinth coffee table that echoes the sunken seating next to the Barbican lake.

Other furniture pieces include a dining table and chairs, two sofas, and shelving and storage.

Read:

Takero Shimazaki Architects infuses Barbican flat with Japanese details

Among the accessories is the Brute Rug, which takes visual cues from an original show flat designed by Howitt in 1967, in which she paired plain off-white flats with bold patterned carpets.

It is made from hand-tufted wool with a long shag pile, which the team said was intended "to deliver a retro feel".

The final pieces in the collection are a series of cushions and textile wall art, each depicting the facades and elevations from the estate.

Warm, neutral tones including mossy greens and rusty oranges are used throughout the collection for a mid-century look, contrasted with stained ash and chrome accents.

To celebrate the launch, Made.com will be curating an installation at the Barbican Centre from 12 September that both showcases the collection and interiors of homes at the Barbican.

Other Barbican news recently featured on Dezeen includes the upcoming revamp of the complex by British architecture studios Allies and Morrison and Asif Khan Studio, and a 30-tonne earthen installation at the estate by Delcy Morelos, which was informed by a mother's womb.

The photography is by Felix Speller.

item.content:encoded:
Game developer Blue Hood Games has released a survival game named Europe Heatwave Simulator, where players need to outlast a 14-day heatwave without air conditioning in an apartment in Paris.

Playable on the Steam platform, which is downloadable for Windows desktops, Europe Heatwave Simulator challenges players to survive a fortnight in a Parisian apartment in 42-degree Celsius heat.

In the game, players navigate life without air conditioning, tending to the needs of their overheating body by keeping cool, hydrated and fed, while also working a remote job from a laptop on the dining table.

Blue Hood Games described Europe Heatwave Simulator as a "dark humour" game centred on "the crushing reality of modern European summers without air conditioning".

Featuring a low-polygon graphic style modelled on early PlayStation games, key decisions in the gameplay include whether to open windows and let mosquitoes in or keep them shut and sacrifice natural airflow.

Players can also order overpriced fans, ice packs and gadgets from a company named Greedco, which bears a swooshing arrow logo similar to that of online retailer Amazon.

Read:

"Human refrigerator" provides escape from deadly heatwaves

In a trailer for Europe Heatwave Simulator, Blue Hood Games described the game as "based on real events" while showing a portion where players race and battle against shoppers to get their hands on air conditioning units, which takes place in a supermarket with branding akin to Lidl.

Severe heatwaves have continued to affect countries across Europe this summer. France experienced record-breaking temperatures in May and June, which contributed to the subsequent spread of wildfires in the country.

Other games that have recently featured on Dezeen include a magazine cover with a built-in paper-thin Tetris game and a retro arcade game by artist collective The Secret Handshake, which was designed as a commentary on Donald Trump's "insane undeclared war" on Iran.

item.content:encoded:
The fifth edition of Bali's Jia Curated design festival features pavilions that aim to put nature at the centre, including structures built from rice husks and salt bricks. Here are eight of the most interesting.

Taking place from 13 to 17 August, this year's Jia Curated showcased craft and design works from Indonesia across Asia including participants from Philippine, Japan and Taiwan.

The festival's new venue at Pengembak Beach in Sanur on Bali's eastern shoreline informed this year's theme – Nature Weave.

The pavilions were each designed to respond to the landscape, creating experiences that allowed materials, objects and structures to actively engage with the surrounding environment.

Each pavilion also combined pieces and input from multiple brands. According to Jia Curated co-founder Budiman Ong, the spirit of mutual co-operation followed the Indonesian principle of Gotong Royong – collective effort.

"We are interested in creating the conditions for spontaneous encounters, encouraging conversation and allowing different disciplines, materials, practices and perspectives to exist alongside one another," said Ong.

"Ultimately, Jia Curated is not simply about showcasing individual works," he continued. |It is about building connection, between designers, craftspeople, brands, institutions and communities across Indonesia and beyond."

Read on for more about the top eight pavilions:

The Intelligence of Surfaces, by DDAP Architect for Lamitak

Local architecture studio DDAP Architect designed the pavilion for decorative high-pressure laminates manufacturer Lamitak to evoke unfolding origami.

The front of the pavilion folded inward, naturally marking the entrance as well as forming a public gathering area.

Perorated timber facade allowed free flow of air within the space, while also doubled as displays for product samples.

The Internal layout followed the journey of how natural paper engineered and crafted into decorative surface, with exisiting landscape integrated into the spacial experience.

Trees punctured the roof, and natural rocks became seatings, creating a conversation between nature, material, and architecture.

"More than an exhibition, the pavilion is an invitation to navigate a new perspective, to questions assumptions, uncover hidden value, and discover that the most meaningful stories often lie beneath the surface," said DDAP Architect.

Sraya, by ATMA for Suaru

Named after the Sanskrit word for shelter, local architecture studio ATMA designed the pavilion for independent furniture brand Suaru to foster a sense of comfort, order and belonging.

The pavilion was arranged into a series of zones that was informed by Asta Kosala Kosali – a spacial philosophy used in a typical Balinese home. It categorises spaces from most to least sacred, combined with the directional axes of north to south and east to west, positioned around a central courtyard.

Objects were placed throughout the pavilion according to the roles traditionally assigned to each space, creating a subtle dialogue between the objects and their architectural setting.

Main Main, by Blanco Studio and Bali Landscape Company

Balinese architecture practice Blanco Studio's pavilion aimed to awaken the nostalgic memories of childhood playtime.

Four raw teak slabs by custom woodworking atelier Kalpa Taru formed a series of communal tables at the centre, on which game boards were free to play.

The studio designed a structure from timber offcuts that rose above the tables to form a tree-like canopy that sheltered the visitors.

"Like the trees we once gathered beneath, it provides shade, shelter and a sense of wonder," said Blanco Studio. "It evokes the simple joy of outdoor play and the quiet nostalgia of childhood afternoon spent together —moments of connection, imagination, and discovery held beneath a protected canopy of nature."

Suar, by Studio Aliri

Indonesia design practice Studio Aliri designed Suar to reference the limited land available in densely populated Indonesian cities and show how spatial richness can be achieved with a limited footprint.

The structure was built on a plot of 2.4 metres long and 4.8 metres wide, with four viewing platforms stacked above one another, all pointing towards the ocean. The first level platform was extended further to connect to the Penjor – a tall, curved bamboo pole used in Balinese Hindu ceremony.

The pavilion was constructed from rubberwood glulam, with safety railings made from woven rattan.

After the festival, the pavilion will be relocated to Medewi Beach in Bali to be permanently used as a public lookout.

Bhumi Lingsir, by Nawangseta, in collaboration with Living Designs Bali

Bali-based architecture studio Nawangseta designed a sequence of spaces informed by traditional Balinese architecture.

The journey began in a space symbolising purity before gradually leading towards areas that represented complexity, duality and the many choices encountered throughout life.

A hundred traditional Balinese Topeng Buduh masks were added to signify the many faces of human nature; sand on the ground embodied both strength and fragility; and water falling from the rain chains symbolised the element that connects all life forms.

"Architectural elements do more than define physical boundaries they communicate philosophical ideas about the relationship between humanity, nature, and spirituality," said Nawangseta.

Oaken Tiltroom, by Spatial Sonata

Constructed from Himalayan salt bricks from Tuscany Stone Boutique, the Oaken Tiltroom pavilion was partially embedded into the ground.

Designed by Jakarta-based design practice Spatial Sonata, the pavilion aimed to create a contemplative environment shaped by landscape and sensory design.

Inside, the pavilion featured Oaken's fragrances as well as Stillroom's botanical drinks, with the aim of engaging all senses.

Alunan Pesisir, by Vivere Group and Eugenio Hendro

Indonesian interiors brand Vivere Group and furniture designer Eugenio Hendro presented a pavilion that aimed to explore the living rhythm of Bali's ever-changing coastline.

Made from glulam, the structure was topped with a curved roof. The ceiling was covered in a blue carpet, while a combination of natural rattan and acoustic panels made by recycled materials formed the side barriers.

The interplay of light and shadow completed the experience where material, form, atmosphere and movement flow as one.

Tapak Tumbuh, by Eugenio Hendro

Created by Indonesian furniture designer Eugenio Hendro, the Tapak Tumbuh pavilion was organised into three chapters: earth, harvest and vegetation.

Ceramic surfaces by Singres tiles, informed by soil formation and agricultural terrain, captured the natural colour and texture of the earth. Decking, facade and walls were made primarily from rice husks and recycled plastic supplied by Plana.

Moire Rugs transformed vegetation by translating the growth of roots, leaves, and organic forms into experimental textile patterns. Large scale rugs spread across the space like living organism.

"From soil with natural hues, sediments and textures. From rices as it grows, harvested, and returns to the land. From roots, leaves, and vegetation that continue to spread and evolve," said Hendro. "These cycles are reinterpreted into surfaces, structures, textiles and spacial experience, each shaped through human hands as an essential catalyst."

The photography is by David Wilson unless otherwise stated.

Jia Curated 2026 took place from 13 to 17 August 2026 at Pengembak Beach in Bali. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Designer Shahar Livne has created The Devil's Milk, a collection of designs that investigate rubber production and its history of violence and abuse.

The designs, which Livne created over two years, include a scale, a cabinet and a bench, made from different types of rubber.

"The concept behind the Devil's Milk project was to investigate the history of rubber production and its material, political, and social cultures," Livne told Dezeen.

"Rubber production and extraction have a long history of abuse and violence, and that is almost forgotten when we see rubber in everyday context," she continued. "Rubber is an essential part of many products and technologies; it has shaped human culture far more than it gets credit for."

Livme sourced the natural latex for the scales and the rubber used for the cabinet from Indonesia, while the bench was made from synthetic rubber used in the film industry.

"During the two years of working on the project, I found many parallels between the human body and the botanical body of the rubber tree," she explained.

"I focused on the idea of botanical kinship – the relationship, indigenous knowledge and spiritual connections humans have with rubber, in this case natural rubber from rubber plants, but also the place of synthetic rubbers in pop culture and fetish, such as in the movie industry."

All of the pieces were designed to involve rubber in different ways. For the cabinet, Livne used wood from the bark of the rubber tree Heave Brislius, which is considered cheap wood and has many imperfections.

"I wanted not only to highlight and elevate the expressiveness of the scars and character of the wood in the furniture piece; it is also symbolic," Livne said.

"The wood inlays decorating the cabinet are made of European, African, Indonesian and South American wood species – all places where rubber wood was extracted from or exported to, and by embedding them in the rubber wood, they 'colonise' it."

Read:

Shahar Livne designs fossil-like jewellery for Balenciaga from ocean plastic

For the bench, which was designed to resemble a log, Livne chose a synthetic engineered rubber material. This was designed to mimic human skin and is used in special effects for props and costumes.

"I used the technique of painting and creating textures in the rubber to create a transition between a human and a tree," Livne said.

"It is inspired by the idea of botanical kinship, the philosophical and ecological world-view that recognises plants as our biological and spiritual relatives rather than mere resources."

She aimed for the piece to challenge "the colonial 'plant blindness' of Western-centric hierarchies that view nature as passive or inferior," Livne said.

"In the many places where the rubber tree grows naturally, such as in the Congo, Borneo and the Amazon, the relationship with the forest is historically spiritual," she continued.

"It is a living space where trees hold divine forces. Here, collecting from the forest is not an 'economic activity'; it is a social interaction with a conscious, sacred environment."

With the scales, Livne wanted to symbolise the economic force of rubber, which she says at one point was compared in its value to precious metals.

"It was aggressively extracted to fuel global industrialisation during the rubber boom in the 19th and 20th centuries," Livne said.

"However, this immense wealth relied entirely on brutal exploitation; raw yields were strictly weighed on scales to enforce strict labour quotas and control Indigenous populations, deforming their bodies."

The title of her project comes from author John Tully's book The Devil's Milk: A social history of rubber, which Livne used as part of her research.

She is currently working on a publication based on her research together with curator Yev Kravt and design studio Droog, who hosted a symposium on rubber with Livne last year.

Livne was named emerging designer of the year at Dezeen Awards 2020 and has previously designed fossil-like jewellery from ocean plastic and trainers from slaughterhouse waste.

The photography is by Barbara Medo.

item.content:encoded:
Chilean studio Iragüen Viñuela Arquitectos has used glued-laminated timber for the House by Fuy River in the Andean foothills, designed as a vertically organised structure that engages with "different layers of the forest canopy".

Nestled in a temperate rainforest in the Andean foothills, the house was designed as a nature retreat for a couple based in Santiago who sought a place where they could be immersed in nature and host family and friends.

The home sits on an 8,000-square-metre site near the Huilo-Huilo, a biological reserve in southern Chile. The property borders the Fuy River, which gave the project its name.

For a clearing in the woods, Iragüen Viñuela Arquitectos conceived a 150-square-metre home that blends with the terrain.

"Its siting, spatial organisation and structural system are guided by a single principle: to minimise intervention while establishing a close relationship between architecture and the surrounding landscape," said the architects.

Rectangular in plan, the House by Fuy River rises three levels and is topped with a hipped roof. Rather than spreading out across the site, the team went vertical to reduce disruption to the landscape.

"This approach minimises the building's footprint and preserves the surrounding native vegetation, avoiding unnecessary intervention in the landscape," the team said.

Exterior walls feature a mix of pre-painted metal cladding and glazed curtain walls. Throughout, the team opted for low-maintenance materials that are well-suited to the climate.

The structure is made entirely of mass timber – specifically, glue-laminated elements made using a CNC machine and prefabricated off-site as "a kit of large structural components".

"The building's defining architectural element is its structure," the team said.

Individual components – beams, columns and diagonal braces – were assembled at the construction site. However, the full-height structural frames, which form the east and west facades, were transported to the site fully assembled.

"This approach reduced construction time in a remote location while ensuring a high level of precision during assembly," the team said.

Within the house, there are large windows, earthy finishes and a division between public and private spaces.

Read:

Croxatto and Opazo Architects perches timber home overlooking Chilean coast

The ground floor holds the entrance, guest rooms and utility spaces, while the first floor contains the "social heart of the house" – the kitchen, dining and living area, all occupying an open-plan room.

The upper floor holds the main bedroom, which is joined by a bathroom and sauna that overlook the forest. The three levels are connected by a central spiral staircase.

"The house is organised vertically to engage with the different layers of the forest canopy, revealing changing conditions of light, vegetation and atmosphere as occupants move through the building," the team said.

Interior finishes included pine board flooring, along with porcelain tiles that are laid over a concrete radiant floor.

Outside of the house, elevated walkways connect to a parking area, storage building and woodshed. The house also features an elevated outdoor terrace with a hot tub, large table and outdoor shower.

Other projects by Iragüen Viñuela Arquitectos include a ski cabin with a "skin of wooden planks" and a square-shaped dwelling that explores the "expressive potential" of prefab timber.

Dezeen Showroom: Italian brand Lapalma has collaborated with architect and designer Raffaella Mangiarotti on a new kaleidoscopic palette of colourways for its catalogue.

Lapalma describes its new colour palette, which debuted at Salone del Mobile, as a "chromatic alphabet" of 16 distinct shades that can be applied to a spectrum of its products.

Existing colours Bianco, Tortora, Mattone, Celeste, Pistacchio, Perla and Nero are joined by nine new shades: Sabbia, Limone, Corallo, Borgogna, Cannella, Oltremare, Alloro, Calce and Gru.

Each was developed by Mangiarotti following research into the brand's historic use of colour, and is designed to work harmoniously across metal, wood and plastic.

The brand aims for the New Colour System to become a practical design tool, enabling seating and tables to share the same aesthetic language while retaining different forms, functions and materials.

"The palette does more than replace or update the brand's historic colours," said Lapalma. "It rethinks them within a more coherent and flexible system, making them easier to combine: this is colour as language, far beyond decoration."

The art direction is by Alberto Mora and the photography is by Salva López.

item.content:encoded:
Polish architect Kuba Woźniczka has completed Studzienno 27, a series of four holiday cabins nestled in the woodlands of the Stołowe Mountains National Park.

Looking to protect the natural landscape as much as possible, Woźniczka – a co-founder of studio KameleonLab – chose to "deliberately limit" the scheme's footprint.

The design left 85 per cent of the site untouched and restricted construction to existing clearings and meadows.

"From the outset, the ambition was not to maximise the site's development potential, but to create a place that would coexist with the surrounding landscape instead of dominating it," the architect told Dezeen.

"The brief focused less on a specific architectural language and more on the values the project should represent: restraint, longevity and respect for the site's existing natural character," he said.

"Although planning regulations would have permitted much denser development, a significant portion of the site was deliberately left untouched, with not a single tree being cut down."

Each of the mono-pitched cabins offers 85 square metres of living space across two storeys.

A living, dining and kitchen area sits alongside a bedroom and bathroom on the ground floor, with an additional bedroom and bathroom upstairs.

Built from cross-laminated timber (CLT), the cabins were oriented to capture views from a balcony and decked patio, while avoiding disruption to any existing trees or vegetation.

Contrasting their exteriors, which are clad in planks of blackened timber, the pale CLT structure has been left exposed throughout the interiors.

Read:

HOLA Design builds gabled lakeside cottage in Poland

The interiors were designed by Wrocław-based interior design practice Madde Studio to create a feeling of "calm and immersion".

Exposed timber walls and ceilings are complemented by pale pastel green tones, with darker green metal frames surrounding the large windows, which have discreet bird-safe markings to minimise collisions.

Alongside areas of bespoke timber carpentry, such as in the kitchens and bathrooms, Madde Studio also sourced a series of vintage and second-hand furniture pieces.

"Rather than resisting the natural ageing process of timber, the project embraces it, allowing the buildings to evolve alongside the surrounding landscape," said Madde Studio.

"Furnishings follow the same philosophy, combining natural materials with carefully selected second-hand furniture and vintage pieces that bring an existing history into the project," it added.

Other holiday retreats in Poland include a duo of cottages overlooking the Silesian Beskids mountains by architecture studio Mistovia, and a gabled lakeside cottage by HOLA Design.

The photography is by Maja Bułkowska.
